analysis.one_liner: Extends federal workplace safety and health protections to incarcerated workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of people incarcerated in federal, state, local, and private-contract prisons work — in prison industries, kitchens, laundries, and work-release jobs — but under the 1970 workplace safety law they are not counted as 'employees,' so no safety inspector is responsible for them. This bill would bring incarcerated workers under federal workplace safety rules, require annual reports on injuries and unsafe conditions at prisons, condition federal public-safety grants on states protecting incarcerated workers, and fund grants to help states rewrite their own safety laws. It was introduced in May 2023 and never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one to two million incarcerated people who work in federal, state, local, and private prisons, often for pennies per hour, would gain the same legal safety protections as other workers — safe equipment, hazard rules, injury reporting, and an agency responsible for enforcement. State agencies would get $20 million a year in grants to build and enforce those protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Incarcerated workers in prisons and jails

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Occupational Safety and Health Act to cover incarcerated workers in state-run and private-contract facilities, and requires states with approved safety plans to include them within two years. [S3]

Requires the federal Bureau of Prisons to apply its workplace safety program to incarcerated workers the same way it applies to staff, and to report annually on injuries, deaths, and safety violations. [S3]

States and localities receiving Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance public-safety grants must certify they protect incarcerated workers, and $20 million of the grants is reserved each year to set up and enforce those protections. [S3]
Creates a separate Department of Labor grant program, authorized at $20 million a year for six years, to help states amend and enforce their safety laws for incarcerated workers. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Private prison operators, state prison industries, and state and local correctional agencies would bear compliance costs — equipment upgrades, hazard abatement, inspections, and annual reporting. Federal taxpayers fund the new grant programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison operators and state corrections agencies

drawbacks.text: Compliance would cost money at facilities that are already underfunded: corrections agencies and prison industries would need to retrofit equipment, run inspections, and file annual safety reports, and some of that cost would fall on state and local budgets. [S3]

The bill ties existing federal public-safety grants to a new state mandate, which critics of conditions on federal funding could reasonably oppose as federal overreach into state corrections policy. [S3]
Incarcerated workers are typically paid little or nothing for their labor, so safety rules alone would not address the pay side of prison work; the bill leaves wages untouched. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: people working in prisons face genuine hazards — heat, machinery, chemicals — with no OSHA coverage today, and this would create enforceable protections and annual public reporting on injuries and violations. The costs are modest relative to that, mostly compliance spending by corrections systems and roughly $20 million a year in federal grants, but the bill leaves the underlying pay issue of prison labor unaddressed, so it is a partial fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and Workforce and Judiciary committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, with eight original Democratic cosponsors. [S1]
The House referred it to both the Education and Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed. [S5]
It gathered 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican signed on. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison operators, prison industries, and state corrections systems are better off because the bill died: they continue operating incarcerated-work programs with no federal safety oversight, no injury reporting, and no enforcement obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison operators and state corrections agencies

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on; the Republican-chaired committees that controlled the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: Operators of facilities under federal, state, and local contracts would have had to bring incarcerated work programs under safety standards, report injuries, and face potential noncompliance findings — new costs on a business model that currently faces no such oversight.

industries.industry: State prison industries (including the federal UNICOR program)
industries.note: Prison industries that use incarcerated labor in factories, furniture, and textile work would face safety compliance costs they are currently exempt from.
They would take on two-year deadlines, annual safety reports, and enforcement duties, but would also receive reserved Byrne grant funds and Labor Department grants to pay for building those programs.
